entry: Class of psychoactive drugs that increase alertness. Stimulants have been used to enhance attention, motivation, cognition, mood and physical activity, and to treat narcolepsy, [[Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder|attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)]], obesity, depression and fatigue. Some occur in nature, such as [[Caffeine]] and [[Nicotine]], while others, including [[Amphetamine]] and [[Methylphenidate]], are synthetic. Stimulants often increase the synaptic concentrations of excitatory neurotransmitters such as norepinephrine and [[Dopamine]]. Effects range from mild stimulation to euphoria, depending on the drug, dose and route of administration. Adverse effects include [[Addiction]], psychosis, anxiety, insomnia and cardiovascular disease, and some stimulants are subject to government regulation or prohibition. Archaeological evidence from Peru shows that [[Cocaine]] use dates back as far as 8000 BC.

English musician, songwriter, actor and activist. He was the lead vocalist, principal songwriter and bassist of the rock band [[The Police|the Police]] (1977–1984, 2007–2008). He began a solo career in 1985, and his music has included elements of rock, jazz, reggae, classical and worldbeat. Sting has sold more than 100 million records as a solo artist and with the Police, and has received 17 [[Grammy Awards]] as both. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2003 as a member of the Police. [[Elizabeth II|Queen Elizabeth II]] made him a CBE for services to music.

Group of rays, a type of cartilaginous fish, in the suborder Myliobatoidei. Stingrays comprise eleven families and about 220 species in 29 genera, found in coastal tropical and subtropical waters worldwide. Most are demersal, living near the seabed, but some, such as the pelagic stingray and the eagle rays, are pelagic. River stingrays and some whiptail species are restricted to fresh water, while deepwater species live in the deep [[Ocean|ocean]]. Their tails typically bear one or more serrated spines that deliver [[Venom|venom]] for defense. Unregulated fishing has made many species threatened: as of 2013, 45 species were listed by the IUCN as vulnerable or endangered. Stingray teeth are known from the Early [[Cretaceous]] onward.

Closed-cycle regenerative heat engine that converts external heat into mechanical work by cyclically expanding and contracting a permanently sealed gas. Invented by Scottish clergyman Robert Stirling in 1816 as a rival to the [[Steam engine|steam engine]], it was used mainly in low-power domestic applications for over a century. The engine is practically silent because it has no exhaust, and when its shaft is turned it can act as a [[Heat pump|heat pump]]. Investment in renewable energy, especially solar energy, has led to its use in concentrated solar power.

Asymptotic approximation for [[Factorial|factorials]]: for large n, n! is approximately √(2πn)(n/e)ⁿ. It is accurate even for small values of n. The approximation is named after James Stirling, although Abraham de Moivre gave a related, less precise result in 1721. Stirling's contribution in 1730 was to show that the constant is precisely 2π. In computer science, the binary logarithm of the factorial is used, for example in the worst-case lower bound for comparison sorting.

Small mustelid mammal native to [[Eurasia]] and northern [[North America]], also called the Eurasian ermine. Its white winter coat, known as ermine, was used by Catholic monarchs in the 15th century and has long been used on the ceremonial robes of members of the [[House of Lords]]. Stoats hunt small mammals such as voles, mice and rabbits, as well as birds, eggs and occasionally fish or insects. Introduced to [[New Zealand]] in the late 19th century to control rabbits, the stoat has had a devastating effect on native birds, and it was nominated as one of the world's top 100 "worst invaders." Because of its wide circumpolar distribution, it is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. A 2021 study split the former single species into three.

Mathematical object defined as a family of [[Random variable|random variables]], usually indexed by time. Stochastic processes model systems and phenomena that vary randomly, such as the growth of a bacterial population, electrical current fluctuating from thermal noise, or the movement of a gas molecule. Louis Bachelier used the [[Brownian motion|Wiener process]] to model price changes on the [[Paris]] Bourse, and A. K. Erlang used the Poisson process to model the number of phone calls in a given period. Classes include random walks, martingales, Markov processes, Lévy processes and Gaussian processes. Their study draws on [[Calculus]], [[Linear algebra]] and [[Topology]], and it remains an active field of research.

Shares into which the ownership of a [[Corporation|corporation]] is divided, also called capital stock. Each share represents fractional ownership, typically entitling its holder to a proportional share of earnings, liquidation proceeds and voting power. Common stock usually carries voting rights, while preferred stock typically has none but is entitled to dividends before other shareholders. Classes of stock may be issued with enhanced voting rights or priority to profits. New shares dilute existing shareholders but raise cash for the business, and companies can also buy back stock. Stock options issued to employees are not ownership but the right to buy shares later at a set price. Stock is traded privately or on [[Stock exchange|stock exchanges]], and private trading is closely overseen by governments to prevent fraud and protect investors.

Marketplace where stockbrokers and traders buy and sell securities such as shares of [[Stock|stock]], [[Bond (finance)|bonds]] and [[Derivative (finance)|derivatives]]. A security must be listed on an exchange to trade there, and trading is generally restricted to member brokers. Exchanges often operate as continuous auction markets, with trades made by open outcry on a trading floor or through electronic systems. New issues are sold in the primary market, and later trading takes place in the secondary market. Electronic communication networks, alternative trading systems and "dark pools" have taken much trading activity away from traditional exchanges. Venetian lenders of the 14th century sold debt issues to individual investors, and the Amsterdam Stock Exchange is often considered the oldest modern securities market. Some scholars argue that a share market existed in [[Ancient Rome]].

Capital and most populous city of [[Sweden]], with about 1 million people in the municipality and 1.6 million in the urban area. The city stretches across fourteen islands where Lake Mälaren flows into the [[Baltic Sea]]. Founded as a city in 1252 by Birger Jarl, it is the cultural, media, political and economic center of Sweden and the largest urban area in the [[Nordic countries]]. The Stockholm region accounts for over a third of the country's GDP. The city hosts the annual [[Nobel Prize]] ceremonies and is home to the Karolinska Institute and KTH Royal Institute of Technology. The Stockholm Metro, opened in 1950, is known for the decor of its stations. The city hosted the 1912 Summer Olympics. The area has been settled since the [[Stone Age]]. Stockholm Palace is the official residence of the monarch, and the Swedish government and parliament sit in the city.

Relationships between the quantities of reactants and products in chemical reactions, based on the law of conservation of mass. Because these relationships form ratios of positive integers, the amount of a product can be calculated from known reactant quantities. For example, one mole of [[Methane]] reacts with two moles of [[Oxygen]] to yield one mole of [[Carbon dioxide]] and two moles of [[Water|water]]. For gases, volume ratios are ideally the same as the ratios of the reactants, by the [[Ideal gas law]]. The term was first used by Jeremias Benjamin Richter in 1792.

Hellenistic philosophy and practical guide to living, founded by Zeno of Citium in [[Athens]] around 300 BCE. Stoics believed the universe operates according to reason, or *logos*, and held that [[Virtue|virtue]] is the highest good and sufficient for a well-reasoned life. The philosophy is traditionally divided into logic, physics and ethics. Stoic ethics stressed self-discipline, emotional self-control and living in accordance with nature, and it distinguished what lies within one's control from what does not. Chrysippus, the third head of the school, shaped its system, and Stoic propositional logic was one of the two great systems of logic in the classical world. Stoicism was widely followed by educated elites in the Roman Empire, including [[Marcus Aurelius]], and it declined after Christianity became the state religion in the 4th century CE. It has since been revived in Renaissance Neostoicism and has inspired modern cognitive therapies.

Pore in the epidermis of plant leaves and stems, bordered by a pair of guard cells that regulate its opening. Carbon dioxide used in [[Photosynthesis]] and oxygen used in respiration pass through stomata by diffusion, while water vapor leaves through them in [[Transpiration]]. Plants therefore cannot take in carbon dioxide without losing water. Stomata occur in the sporophyte of most land plants, though not in [[Liverwort|liverworts]]. Most tree species have them only on the lower leaf surface, whereas [[Monocotyledon|monocotyledons]] such as onion, oat and maize often have about the same number on both surfaces. Many desert plants that use crassulacean acid metabolism open their stomata at night, when water evaporates more slowly, to reduce water loss. Size varies by species, but lengths range from 10 to 80 μm end to end.

Muscular, hollow digestive organ in the upper gastrointestinal tract of humans and many other animals, including some invertebrates. It lies between the [[Esophagus]] and the [[Small intestine]], where digestive [[Enzyme|enzymes]] and gastric acid begin the chemical breakdown of food. Parietal cells secrete [[Hydrochloric acid|hydrochloric acid]] and intrinsic factor, which is needed for absorption of [[Vitamin B12]] in the small intestine. The pyloric sphincter releases partly digested food, called chyme, into the duodenum. The stomach normally holds about one liter of food, and its folded lining allows it to expand. It is divided into four regions: the cardia, fundus, body and pylorus, and it is supplied by the [[Vagus nerve]].

American media personality, actor and retired [[Professional wrestling|professional wrestler]], born Steven James Anderson. As "Stone Cold" Steve Austin, he became the most popular wrestler of the Attitude Era from 1997 to 2001, feuding with [[Vince McMahon]] and [[Bret Hart]]. He won the WWF Championship six times and the Royal Rumble a record three times, in 1997, 1998 and 2001. Forced to retire from in-ring competition in 2003 after multiple knee injuries and a serious neck injury, he remains an ambassador for [[WWE]]. He was inducted into the WWE Hall of Fame in 2009 and again in 2025, with Bret Hart.

English and British imperial unit of mass equal to 14 avoirdupois [[Pound (mass)|pounds]] (about 6.35 kg). Stones were formerly standardized for trade in England and other Germanic-speaking countries of northern Europe, with values ranging from about 5 to 40 local pounds. With metrication, they were superseded or adapted to the [[Kilogram|kilogram]] from the mid-19th century. The Weights and Measures Act 1835 permitted a stone of 14 pounds for trade. Today the stone remains in customary use in the [[United Kingdom]] and Ireland, chiefly for body weight.

Prehistoric [[Megalith|megalithic]] monument on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England. Its outer ring of sarsen standing stones, each about 13 feet (4.0 m) high and weighing around 25 tons, is topped by horizontal lintels joined with mortise and tenon joints. Inside are a ring of smaller bluestones and free-standing trilithons. Built in several phases from about 3100 BC to about 1600 BC, the monument is aligned to the sunrise on the [[Summer solstice]] and the sunset on the [[Winter solstice]]. It stands in one of the densest concentrations of [[Neolithic]] and [[Bronze Age]] monuments in England. Deposits of human bone date from as early as 3000 BC, suggesting a burial function from its beginnings. Added to the list of [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Sites in 1986, it is one of the most famous landmarks in the United Kingdom.

Series of spontaneous [[Riot|riots]] and demonstrations against a police raid on the Stonewall Inn, a Mafia-owned bar in Greenwich Village, [[Manhattan|Lower Manhattan]], New York City, in the early hours of June 28, 1969. The riots marked a new beginning for the gay rights movement in the United States and around the world. Protests continued for several nights, and within weeks activist groups had formed to establish places where gay people could be open without fear of arrest. The first anniversary was marked by peaceful demonstrations in several American cities that later grew into pride parades.

Large, long-legged, long-necked wading bird with a long, stout bill, in the family Ciconiidae. Storks have 20 living species in six genera, and many live in drier habitats than related [[Heron|herons]] and [[Ibis|ibises]]. Most eat frogs, fish, insects, earthworms and small birds or mammals, and they communicate at the nest by bill-clattering. Many species migrate, and their soaring flight uses thermal air currents. The marabou stork, with a wingspan of 3.2 m, joins the [[Andean condor]] in having the widest wingspan of any living land bird. Storks are prominent in folklore, especially in Western tradition as deliverers of newborn humans. All 20 species have been assessed by the IUCN, though several assessments rest on incorrect assumptions.

Act of political violence in [[Paris]] on July 14, 1789, and the flashpoint of the [[French Revolution]]. Insurgents tried to seize the medieval armory, fortress and political prison known as the Bastille. After four hours of fighting that left 94 dead, they entered it, and its governor, Bernard-René Jourdan de Launay, was killed after surrendering. The prison held only seven inmates and was scheduled for demolition, but it symbolized royal authority and the monarchy's abuse of power. July 14 is France's national holiday, known in English as Bastille Day.

Appliance or construction that generates heat inside or on top of itself from an energy source, used for [[Cooking|cooking]] or indoor heating. Unlike [[Oven|ovens]], which keep heat in closed chambers, stoves let their heat flow outward. They can burn wood, [[Coal]], [[Natural gas|natural gas]], [[Propane]], oil, kerosene or electricity. Electric and induction stoves are popular in home kitchens because their heat is precisely controlled and they avoid open flames, reducing carbon monoxide buildup and the risk of house fires. Propane and natural-gas stoves are more common in [[Restaurant|restaurants]] because they offer instant, intense heat and durability. Concern about [[Air pollution]] has led to cleaner designs, such as pellet stoves and air-tight stoves that burn fuel more completely.

Water body connecting two seas or water basins, usually a narrow channel between two landmasses. Water can flow through it in either direction at about the same elevation on both sides, though topography generally constricts the flow. Some straits have a dominant directional current, and their sediments form deltas or fans at the exits. Straits are the converse of [[Isthmus|isthmuses]], which connect two large landmasses between oceans. Many are economically important shipping routes, and [[War|wars]] have been fought for control of them. Artificial channels such as the [[Suez Canal]] connect two oceans or seas over land. Some straits are not navigable because they are too narrow or shallow, or because of reefs.

Narrowest part of the [[English Channel]], separating [[Great Britain]] from continental Europe and marking the boundary between the Channel and the [[North Sea]]. The shortest crossing, 20.6 miles (33.2 km), runs from South Foreland near Dover in [[Kent]] to Cap Gris-Nez near Calais. It is one of the world's busiest international seaways, used by over 400 commercial vessels daily and monitored around the clock. A traffic separation scheme became mandatory for vessels over 300 gross tons in 1977, after a chain of disasters in 1971 killed 64 people. The [[Channel Tunnel]], opened in 1994, runs beneath the strait at an average depth of 45 m (148 ft). On a clear day, the White Cliffs of Dover are visible from France.

Strait connecting the [[Atlantic Ocean]] to the [[Mediterranean Sea]] and separating [[Europe]] from [[Africa]]. At its narrowest point, the two continents are 7.7 nautical miles (14.3 km) apart, and ferries cross in as little as 35 minutes. The strait lies in the territorial waters of [[Morocco]], [[Spain]] and the British overseas territory of [[Gibraltar]], and its depth ranges from 300 to 900 meters. Its name derives from the Rock of Gibraltar, from the Arabic *Jabal Ṭāriq*, or "Tariq's Mount." Around 5.97 million years ago the connection was progressively restricted until it closed, during the Messinian salinity crisis; the Atlantic–Mediterranean link was restored about 5.33 million years ago by the Zanclean flood. Foreign vessels and aircraft have freedom of navigation for continuous transit.

Waterway between the [[Persian Gulf]] and the Gulf of Oman, with [[Iran]] on the north coast and the Musandam Peninsula of [[Oman]] on the south. It is about 104 miles (167 km) long and is the only sea passage from the Persian Gulf to the open ocean. During 2023–2025, about 20% of the world's liquefied natural gas and 25% of seaborne oil trade passed through it annually. It is the only maritime route for several Gulf countries, including the [[United Arab Emirates]], [[Qatar]], [[Bahrain]], [[Kuwait]] and [[Iraq]]. Before 2026 the strait had not been closed for an extended period during Middle East conflicts. Iranian blockades that closed the strait became a major focus of the 2026 Iran War and produced the 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis.
